description: "No additional skills required. Our team is already fully staffed with 2 members and ready to compete!"
summary:
On Earth, a flame points up. In space, it becomes a glowing blue ball. NASA-funded ISS tests found materials burning at about 15% oxygen, versus about 18% on Earth, and future Moon habitats may use 34% oxygen. So how do you keep a crew safe?
We built a Colab dashboard that tackles it two ways. An explorer ranks eight NASA fire experiments for the place you care about. A fire-alert simulator lets you slide gravity and oxygen and watch the flame, alert level and water-mist response change.
Every number is tagged NASA reference, calculated, or our assumption, so nothing is hidden. Pilot-tested with 3 users. An educational simulation, not a real alarm system.
details: 1. What does it do, and how does it work? Fire in Free-Fall is a Google Colab dashboard with two parts. The research explorer summarizes eight NASA combustion experiments (BASS-II, SoFIE-MIST, Saffire, MIST, FLEX, SAME, ACME, LUCI) and ranks them for a chosen place (ISS or Moon/Mars habitat) and topic (flammability limits, smoke detection, suppression). The fire-alert simulator updates every 0.1 s: heat in and out sets the temperature, temperature sets a risk score, and the risk triggers Level 1–3 alerts, water-mist spraying and venting. Users slide gravity and watch the flame change from a blue sphere to a tall flame. 2. How is it useful? It turns scattered research into something a student or engineer can explore in minutes. It shows why a high-oxygen habitat changes the fire problem: in our simulation of a fuel leak, the fire takes longer to go out at 34% oxygen than at 21% (about 70 s versus 65 s, peak temperature about 216 °C versus 198 °C). 3. What business or real-world impact does it aim for? We do not claim commercial results. It is an educational and early-design prototype. Possible paths are teaching tools for schools and space outreach, a quick-look aid for habitat safety teams, and a template for exploring other hazard research. Water-mist suppression developed for the ISS is also used on Earth, as the challenge itself points out. 4. What tools did we use? Python in Google Colab with numpy, pandas, matplotlib and ipywidgets. Data came from NASA Technical Reports Server papers, NASA fact sheets and a NASA-funded SoFIE-MIST report. AI assistance (Claude) helped with source searching and code drafting. (Keep this line only if it is true for your team. Space Apps asks teams to disclose AI use.) 5. What makes it creative? Every number wears a label: Reference (cited NASA source), Calculated (formula shown) or Design (our assumption). Nothing is passed off as measured. One slider links gravity to flame shape, so the physics is visible, not just described. Two oxygen thresholds: the fire goes out at 15% (from ISS tests), but venting continues to a 4% floor in the sealed zone, a design choice we kept separate. A built-in self-test prints ALL TESTS PASSED, so judges can verify the model. 6. What did the team consider? Validity: we checked key values against the source documents and marked what we could not verify. Honest limits: the 15% figure comes from specific materials; the 8.2 psia / 34% habitat is NASA's recommended atmosphere, not a final spec; the ethanol baseline is the 2013–2014 average. Safety realism: 4% oxygen cannot sustain life, so it applies only to an unoccupied sealed compartment. Audience: students to engineers; one-click Run all, no installation. Evidence of use: a pilot test with 3 users.
